newsitem.title: UK: Jolly Rancher sweets ad draws rebuke for drug link.
newsitem.headline: Jolly Rancher sweets ad draws rebuke for drug link.

text.p: Two poster advertisements for Jolly Rancher sweets have drawn a rebuke for using headlines that could be interpreted as condoning drug use, the Advertising Standards Authority said on Wednesday.

The ads, created for Jolly Rancher maker Leaf United Kingdom Ltd, part of Finnish Huhtamaki Oy HUHK.HE, by Banks Hoggins O'Shea, featured a person's open mouth with a square blue sweet on the tongue. One advert carried the headline, Fancy a smack in the mouth, and the second ad was headlined, Always read instructions before use.

The Advertising Authority, which registered 11 complaints to the ad including one from a member of Parliament, said, "...the advertisements could be seen as condoning drugs." The industry regulatory body said it asked Leaf United not to use the adverts again and to adopt a different approach in the future.
The Advertising Authority upheld complaints against two separate advertisements that were found to be sexually offensive.

An advert for Loaded magazine, which appeared in 90 Minutes magazine, was found offensive for showing actress Danniella Westbrook clad in a negligee and sucking a lollipop. The bottom of the ad showed a picture of the magazine and the same picture of Westbrook with the line, "Suck this."
In upholding the complaint, the Advertising Authority noted the actress had her hand on the top of her thigh and said the innuendo and the phrase "suck this" were offensive.

An advert in the Surrey & West Hants Star newspaper for the Pantiles Club & Restaurant, was cited for showing a woman wearing partially undone shorts and with her arms partially covering her naked breasts. The ad offered an "invitation" to a "shorts and t-shirt party." The Advertising Authority found the ad unacceptable and likely to cause offense.

The Advertising Authority also upheld a complaint against Virgin Interactive Entertainment for a poster advert for a computer game. The ad showed a white bathtub filled with blood that was spilling over onto the floor. The Advertising Authority said the ad "went beyond the bounds of acceptability for a poster in its graphic depiction of a macabre image."
But complaints were not upheld over two public service advertisements -- one over the negative portrayal of disabled people and one over a claim of sexual abuse.

Two poster adverts for the UK Department of Transport, created by the DMB&B agency to discourage drink driving, showed a disabled man being fed or given a drink, with the line, Drinking and driving wrecks lives. One ad said, How would you like to do nothing with the rest of your life? The second ad said, You'll never have to think about what to wear on a Saturday night.

Complainants said the ads were offensive to the disabled and implied that the disabled can do nothing and are worthless. But the Advertising Authority found the ads were not objectionable and were not intended to offend.

The Advertising Authority also did not uphold a complaint against the City of Bradford Metropolitan Council for a poster ad showing two young girls playing in a bedroom. "By the time they reach 18, one of them will have been subjected to sexual abuse. Zero tolerance. From flashing to rape, male abuse of power is a crime," the ad said.
Although complainants said the ad was misleading, the Advertising Authority said the sexual abuse claim was acceptable in light of a study listing nine definitions of sexual abuse.
